chunks: Synchronous rectification pros and cons. The question: Explain synchronous rectification. What are its pros/cons?
Synchronous rectification means replacing the buck's freewheel diode with a second MOSFET. This MOSFET turns on when the main switch turns off, and carries the inductor current.
A diode wastes a fixed voltage drop. A transistor acts like a small resistor, so it wastes much less.
Picture a turnstile versus an open gate. A diode is a turnstile: everyone who walks through must push against a stiff bar, which costs effort.
A transistor is an open gate with a little friction.

The catch is that someone must open and close the gate on time, which costs a little effort, and it must never be open at the same moment as the main switch, or current would rush straight through both.
The only change from the diode buck is that the diode's job is done by Q 2 (with its body diode drawn). G L is driven as the complement of G H , with dead time.
The inductor current is positive when it flows from SW into L ; if it goes negative, it flows from C out back through L into Q 2 .
Synchronous rectifier: a transistor doing the job of a diode, timed by the controller. Forward drop: the voltage across a conducting diode, about 0. 3 to 0.
5 volts for a Schottky. R DS(on) : a transistor's small resistance when fully on.
Dead time: a brief gap so the two transistors never conduct together ("Shoot-through and dead time").
Diode emulation: turning the low-side transistor off when its current reaches zero, so it behaves like a diode and saves power at light load.
A 12 volts to 3. 3 volts buck delivers 2 amps, and the lower device conducts 72. 5 percent of the time. A Schottky with a 0. 45 volts drop wastes 0. 45 times 2 times 0.

"Synchronous rectification replaces the freewheel diode with a low-side MOSFET driven complementary to the high side.
It wins on efficiency: loss is I to the 2R DS(on) instead of V f times I , so at 3. 3 volts out and 2 amps you cut roughly 650 milliwatts to about 30 milliwatts.

The costs are a second gate driver, dead time to avoid shoot-through with body-diode loss during it, gate-drive power at all loads, and negative inductor current at light load unless you add diode emulation or PFM."
